title: Same-event pairs with the transformer parser
text: Same-event pairs with the transformer parser
why: Independent publishers rarely matched (3.6% exact, 6.2% by embedding) on spaCy small triples; this tests how much of that is the extractor.
acceptance: T66's 563 same-event pairs rerun with en_core_web_trf: exact, entity-pair and embedding match rates for copy and independent pairs, next to the small-parser rates.
steps: Rerun on the same pairs, CPU, isolated venv

text: T72 started

Prediction for T72 (CPU, isolated venv ner_spacy_trf with sentence-transformers and pyarrow added, en_core_web_trf instead of en_core_web_sm, everything else in triple_pairs2.py unchanged: same queue file, same pair rule, same keys, bge-small-en-v1.5 at cosine 0.90; unjudged match rates only): independent pairs rise but stay low: exact match under 0.10 (small parser 0.036), entity-pair match under 0.15 (0.054), embedding match under 0.20 (0.062); copy pairs stay near 0.90 on exact (0.8995); triples per pair rise by at least 20 percent. So the parser is part of the limit but not the main one. A miss would be independent embedding match of 0.20 or more, which would make the extractor the main limit and justify the full rebuild. A second miss would be copy exact rate falling below 0.80 (the new parser producing less stable keys). Judge: match rates, not correctness of the triples.
T72 step 1

Score for T68, run locally on CPU (owner yes), not on Kaggle (the kernel stayed queued about 9 h and never ran): spaCy transformer en_core_web_trf exact F1 0.5589 (P 0.488, R 0.654), overlap F1 0.735, 73 s; GLiNER medium v2.1 exact F1 0.6186 (P 0.567, R 0.680), overlap F1 0.6985, 84 s; Stanza from T67 exact 0.5797, overlap 0.7331; spaCy small 0.5061. Same 1,000 Few-NERD sentences (sha8 395b1f23), type ignored, Wikipedia text not news. Files: runs/t68/local/ner_bakeoff_spacy_trf.json, ner_bakeoff_gliner.json. PREDICTIONS (L1382): spaCy transformer exact between 0.55 and 0.68 HELD (0.559); GLiNER overlap F1 above 0.70 MISSED by a hair (0.6985); GLiNER exact below spaCy transformer MISSED (0.619 against 0.559, the other way round); at least one beats Stanza by 0.02 exact HELD (GLiNER +0.039); finishes in under 45 minutes HELD for the local run (about 10 min plus a 2 min retry), not applicable to the Kaggle kernel. Disclosure: GLiNER's first attempt failed on a missing protobuf package; I installed protobuf and sentencepiece in its isolated venv and reran GLiNER only. Reading: GLiNER is the best open extractor measured here (exact F1 0.619), +0.039 over Stanza, +0.113 over spaCy small. Caveat: Wikipedia text with types ignored; the news-text gap is unmeasured. Acceptance bar (best of the two at least 0.02 above Stanza) met. Next: rebuild triples on GLiNER entities (the spaCy small parse stays for the dependency structure).
T68 step 2
T68 closes step 2 after step 0
T68 closed: GLiNER medium v2.1 exact F1 0.619 on 1,000 Few-NERD sentences, +0.039 over Stanza, so the bar is met; spaCy transformer 0.559. Run locally on CPU, Kaggle kernel never started.

Health loop added (owner: nothing seemed to be running and we were waiting, with no signal): kit/live/health.py, run every 3 minutes by the poller through tick.py, writes a health row with a verdict (BROKEN, WORKING, WAITING naming what it waits on, IDLE) shown on every ledger tab and in the terminal view; tested on fake rows for all six paths (queued only, overdue job not counted as working, fresh job, empty, core piece down, idle). Its first real run caught a finished job (t68-local-cpu) still marked running; both stale T68 rows were closed. Not yet checked: that the poller's own subprocess call stays under the 180 s timeout when T72 holds 12 CPU threads.

Run 1 of T72 crashed at 22:58 (about 4 min in): the transformer tagger raised a blas shape error (zero-width input) on a blank or one-symbol sentence in a cached article. Nothing was scored. The health check flagged it as overdue only after its 10-minute grace, because the process was not watched. Fix: triple_pairs3.py now skips blank sentences, retries a failing article sentence by sentence, and reports the failure counts in its output; the rerun started 23:05 with a watcher that marks the row done or failed the moment the process ends. The prediction at L1483 is unchanged and scored on the rerun only.

Score for T72 (rerun, projects/world-state/triple_pairs3.py, runs/pulse/triple_pairs3_trf.json, CPU, isolated venv, en_core_web_trf instead of en_core_web_sm, everything else as T66; 0 parse failures, 0 sentences skipped; unjudged match rates only). Independent pairs (414 with triples on both sides, 4,187 triples): exact 0.0449, entity-pair 0.0671, embedding 0.0755; small parser (407 pairs, 4,324 triples): 0.0358, 0.0543, 0.0617. Copy pairs (156, 1,628 triples): exact 0.9238, entity-pair 0.9251, embedding 0.9355; small parser (1,752 triples): 0.8995, 0.9018, 0.9098. PREDICTIONS (L1483): independent exact under 0.10 HELD (0.045); entity-pair under 0.15 HELD (0.067); embedding under 0.20 HELD (0.076); copy exact stays near 0.90 and above 0.80 HELD (0.924); triples per pair rise by at least 20 percent MISSED (they fell: 10.4 against 11.2 per copy pair, 10.1 against 10.6 per independent pair, about -5 to -7 percent). READING: the stronger parser lifts independent-publisher agreement by about one point (exact 3.6 to 4.5 percent, embedding 6.2 to 7.6) and does not change the picture: identical facts across independent publishers stay rare under these keys. So the dependency parser is not the main limit; what is left is the rule layer on top of it (the same spo_chains rules) and how entities and predicates are normalised, which is where GLiNER entities and a canonical form come in. Rebuilding every earlier triple count on the transformer parser would not change the conclusion at the scale tested. Judge: match rates, not correctness of the triples. Caveat: same 563 pairs, a sample found by embedding similarity, not all article pairs.
T72 step 2
T72 step 3

T72 closed: with the transformer parser independent-publisher triple agreement is 4.5 percent exact and 7.6 percent by embedding against 3.6 and 6.2 with the small parser; the parser is not the main limit. Four of five predictions held.

title: Entity-canonical matching of same-event triples
text: Entity-canonical matching of same-event triples
why: The parser is not the main limit (T72); test whether normalising subjects and objects to GLiNER entities makes independent publishers' facts match.
acceptance: T66's 563 same-event pairs, small parser, with subject and object mapped to GLiNER entities: entity-pair and entity-pair-plus-predicate match rates for copy and independent pairs next to the text-key rates.
steps: Triples and GLiNER entities extracted, CPU

text: a criterion is over 200 characters
T73 started

Prediction for T73 (CPU; the 563 same-event pairs of T66 and T72 with the same small parser and the same spo_chains rules, so only the keys change; GLiNER medium v2.1 at threshold 0.5 on each triple's sentence; a subject or object phrase maps to an entity when the phrase text contains the entity text or the entity text contains the phrase, case-insensitive, after dropping determiners and possessives; a phrase with no entity keeps its text key; match keys: (a) subject entity + object entity, (b) subject entity + predicate lemma + object entity; unjudged match rates only). Text-key rates to beat, independent pairs: exact 0.036 and entity-pair 0.054 (T66), 0.045 and 0.067 with the transformer parser (T72). PREDICTIONS: (a) independent pairs rise to between 0.08 and 0.15; (b) stays under 0.08; copy pairs (a) stay at 0.90 or above. If (a) reaches 0.15 or more, entity normalisation is a main lever and the next step is canonical predicates; if it stays under 0.08, it is not, and the limit is that independent publishers rarely state the same triple, so matching needs event frames, not triples. Judge: match rates, not correctness. Caveat: a looser mapping rule can inflate matches; the output reports how many phrases mapped to an entity.
T73 step 1

Started 23:2x (CPU, three stages chained by /workspace/data/venvs/run_t73.sh under a 50 min cap): stage 1 t73_extract.py (same pair rule and small parser as T66, writes runs/pulse/t73_triples.json and t73_sentences.json), stage 2 t73_gliner.py (ner_gliner venv, writes t73_entities.json), stage 3 t73_match.py (writes t73_match.json). The text-key rates are recomputed on the same sample in stage 3, so the comparison does not depend on T66's numbers. Process note: the T72 rerun was recorded as failed by the poller although it finished (I had put its process id on the row; the poller, still running old code, closes any row whose process ends without its own finish call, before my watcher ran). This chain keeps the process id off the row and closes the row itself.

First full run lost 23:22-23:44: stage 1 crashed when saving its result (TypeError: Object of type int64 is not JSON serializable; the pair indices a and b were numpy integers), leaving an empty t73_triples.json and no sentences file; the chain closed the row as failed, correctly. I had not smoke-tested the save step. Fix: int(a), int(b). Added NP (number of pairs) and T73DIR (output folder) switches to all three scripts and ran the whole chain on 5 pairs into a scratch folder first: all three stages passed (stage 1 8 min of setup, GLiNER 47 sentences in 4 s, matching in under a second). Those 5-pair numbers are plumbing checks, not evidence, and I did not use them. Full rerun started 23:56 under a 55 min cap. Prediction at L1497 unchanged.

Score for T73 (projects/world-state/t73_match.json, CPU, chain run 23:53-00:07; same 563 pairs and small parser as T66; GLiNER medium v2.1 entities from 4,030 unique sentences; unjudged match rates). Reproduction check: the recomputed text keys equal T66 exactly (independent exact 0.0358, entity-pair 0.0543; copy exact 0.8995). Independent pairs (407, 4,324 triples): subject-entity + object-entity key 0.0386; with predicate lemma 0.0317; text pair key 0.0543; text exact key 0.0358. Copy pairs (156, 1,752 triples): entity pair 0.8933, with predicate 0.8927, text exact 0.8995. About 52 percent of subject and object phrases mapped to an entity. PREDICTIONS (L1497): independent entity-pair between 0.08 and 0.15 MISSED (0.039, lower than the text key 0.054); entity-plus-predicate under 0.08 HELD (0.032); copy entity-pair at 0.90 or above MISSED by a hair (0.893). Why entity keys were lower than text keys: my design mixed key types (a mapped phrase becomes E:entity, an unmapped one stays T:text), so identical text matched less often when GLiNER found an entity in one sentence and not in the other. POST-HOC, not the registered test and labelled so (runs/pulse/t73_posthoc_union.json): match if the text keys are equal OR both sides map to the same entity pair: independent 0.0557 (text pair alone 0.0543), copy 0.9053; entities add only 6 extra matches among 4,324 independent triples and 6 among 1,752 copy triples. READING: normalising subjects and objects to GLiNER entities is not the lever; even in the best case it adds about 0.1 point. With T72 (the parser adds about 1 point) the picture is consistent: independent publishers' triples rarely coincide whatever the keys, so the rule layer is not the bottleneck either; what remains is that independent publishers state different facts or the same fact in different frames. Next candidates, each its own task with a prediction first: event-level matching (same event by trigger and participants, not the same triple), or giving up exact triple support as the Area signal. Judge: match rates, not correctness. Note: the chain's first stage finished far faster than my 20 min estimate (about 8 min).
T73 step 2
T73 step 3

T73 closed: GLiNER-entity keys do not raise independent-publisher triple agreement (0.039 against 0.054 text keys; 0.0557 with a union rule, 6 extra matches in 4,324). One of three predictions held, one missed by a hair, one missed.

title: Partial-triple matching across same-event articles
text: Partial-triple matching across same-event articles
why: Exact triples rarely coincide across independent publishers (T66, T72, T73); test whether two of the three elements do, against a chance control.
acceptance: On the 563 same-event pairs: match rates for predicate+subject, predicate+object and any two of three elements, for copy and independent pairs, next to a control where B comes from an unrelated pair.
steps: Rates computed on the T73 triples

text: T74 started

Prediction for T74 (CPU, computed from runs/pulse/t73_triples.json and t73_entities.json, no new model run; same 563 pairs; an element matches when the text keys are equal or both sides map to the same GLiNER entity; control: each A-side triple is compared with the triples of a B article drawn from a different, random pair of the same group, seed 7, so the control measures chance and common words like said). Rates are the share of A-side triples with a match. PREDICTIONS: independent pairs, predicate lemma + subject: 0.10 to 0.25; predicate lemma + object: 0.05 to 0.20; subject + object: about 0.04 (T73); any two of the three: 0.15 to 0.30; the control rate for any two of the three is under 0.08, so the excess over chance is at least 0.07 for any-two-of-three; copy pairs any two of three: 0.92 or above. A miss would be the control at 0.08 or more, which would mean partial keys mostly match on common words and are not a usable support signal. Judge: match rates, not correctness.
T74 step 1

Score for T74 (projects/world-state/t74_partial.py, runs/pulse/t74_partial.json; computed from the T73 triples and entities, no model run; unjudged). Independent pairs (407 pairs, 4,324 A-side triples), share with a match in the other article: predicate + subject 0.0696, predicate + object 0.0749, subject + object 0.0583, any two of three 0.1110, all three 0.0446. Control (B from a different random pair): predicate + subject 0.0009, predicate + object 0.0023, subject + object 0.0005, any two of three 0.0028, all three 0.0005. Copy pairs (156 pairs, 1,752 triples): any two of three 0.9401, all three 0.9115, control 0.0011. PREDICTIONS: predicate + subject 0.10 to 0.25 MISSED (0.070); predicate + object 0.05 to 0.20 HELD (0.075); subject + object about 0.04 MISSED narrowly (0.058, the union rule); any two of three 0.15 to 0.30 MISSED (0.111); control for any two of three under 0.08 HELD (0.003); excess over chance at least 0.07 HELD (0.108); copy any two of three at 0.92 or above HELD (0.940). READING: partial support is real and not a common-word artifact: 11.1 percent of independent publishers' triples have a two-of-three match in the other same-event article against 0.3 percent by chance (about 40 times chance), and that is 2.5 times the exact all-three rate (4.5 percent). It is still low: nearly nine in ten independent triples find nothing in a same-event article under these keys. My predictions for the partial rates were too high. Candidate Area-support signal, in order of strength: any two of three (0.111), predicate + object, predicate + subject, exact. Next: count support over more than two publishers per event (the earlier T62 to T64 counts used exact strings), and decide what rate of independent support would be enough for an Area; that bar needs the owner (T48). Judge: match rates, not correctness. Caveat: same 563 pairs, a sample found by embedding similarity.
T74 step 2
T74 step 3

T74 closed: two-of-three element matching finds support for 11.1 percent of independent publishers' triples against 0.3 percent by chance, 2.5 times the exact-triple rate; three of seven predictions missed because I set the partial rates too high.

Owner asked for the process to be written up in detail. Written as playbook/16-the-working-loop.md (232 lines, linked from playbook/README.md): the cycle, the round card, smoke test, prediction rules, fixed scoring words, sealed-set rules, job and heartbeat rules, the health check, the trust grid, the two layers of self-improvement with five process numbers and a retrospective, permissions, the failure table from this session, a start-of-round checklist, and a build order. Items marked built exist today; items marked to build or ours are proposals.

title: Replicate T74 on 600 fresh pairs
text: Replicate T74 on 600 fresh pairs
why: T74 found 11.1% two-of-three support on one sample of 563 pairs; check it holds on a disjoint sample before building on it.
acceptance: T74 pipeline on pairs 600 to 1200 of the same shuffled list: independent and copy rates and the chance control, next to T74.
steps: Smoke test then full chain, CPU

text: T75 started

Prediction for T75 (CPU; the same chain as T73 and T74 unchanged, on pairs 600 to 1200 of the same shuffled list of 9,811 same-event pairs, so a disjoint sample; small parser; GLiNER medium v2.1; match rules as in T74; the pair list and embeddings are now cached, the first run builds the cache). PREDICTIONS, independent pairs: any two of three elements 0.09 to 0.13 (T74: 0.111); predicate + subject 0.05 to 0.09; predicate + object 0.05 to 0.10; all three 0.03 to 0.06; the control for any two of three under 0.01; copy pairs any two of three at 0.92 or above; copy share of pairs 0.22 to 0.32 (T74: 0.27). A miss on the two-of-three rate outside 0.07 to 0.15 means the 11% was partly sample luck and the Area support signal is weaker or stronger than T74 said. This is a blind prediction on a new sample; I have not looked at these pairs. Judge: match rates, not correctness.
T75 step 1

Score for T75 (blind, disjoint sample: pairs 600 to 1200 of the same shuffled list; runs/pulse/t75/t74_partial.json; the smoke test passed on 5 pairs, then the full chain ran with the pair cache built on the first run). Independent pairs (397 pairs, 4,351 triples), share with a match in the other article, against T74 (407 pairs, 4,324 triples): any two of three 0.1112 against 0.1110; predicate + subject 0.0637 against 0.0696; predicate + object 0.0786 against 0.0749; subject + object 0.0609 against 0.0583; all three 0.0453 against 0.0446; control (B from a different random pair) any two of three 0.0028 against 0.0028. Copy pairs (170 pairs, 1,811 triples): any two of three 0.9321 against 0.9401, all three 0.9006 against 0.9115; copy share of pairs 0.2998 against 0.2771. Exact and entity keys (stage 3 of the same chain): independent text exact 0.0377, text pair 0.0577, entity pair 0.0448 (T73: 0.0358, 0.0543, 0.0386). PREDICTIONS (blind): any two of three 0.09 to 0.13 HELD (0.111); predicate + subject 0.05 to 0.09 HELD (0.064); predicate + object 0.05 to 0.10 HELD (0.079); all three 0.03 to 0.06 HELD (0.045); control under 0.01 HELD (0.003); copy any two of three at 0.92 or above HELD (0.932); copy share 0.22 to 0.32 HELD (0.300). Seven of seven. READING: the T74 finding is not sample luck. About 11 percent of independent publishers' triples find a two-of-three match in a same-event article, against 0.3 percent by chance, on two disjoint samples of about 400 pairs each; exact all-three support is about 4.5 percent; entity keys again add nothing over text keys. The Area support signal is stable at about 11 percent for pairs. Caveat: both samples come from the same shuffled list of embedding-found pairs; a different time window or source mix has not been tested. Note: two of the seven predictions were wide enough that a hit says little (copy share, copy any two); the five independent-pair predictions are the informative ones.
T75 step 2
T75 step 3
T75 closed: the two-of-three support rate for independent publishers replicates on a disjoint sample (0.1112 against 0.1110; control 0.003); seven of seven blind predictions held.

title: Triple support across many independent publishers
text: Triple support across many independent publishers
why: Pairs give 11% two-of-three support (T74, T75); an Area needs several independent publishers. Count how many back a triple.
acceptance: Share of triples backed by 1, 2, 3 or more independent same-event articles, by number of partners, next to a random-partner control.
steps: Smoke test then full run, CPU

text: T76 started

Prediction for T76 (blind, CPU; the cached 9,811 same-event pairs; articles with at least 2 same-event partners, 3,460 of them, and their partners about 3,980 articles to parse with the small parser; a partner is independent when its shingle Jaccard with the article is under 0.30; a triple is supported by a partner when one of that partner's triples agrees on two of subject key, predicate lemma and object key; text keys only; control: the same number of random articles; unjudged match rates). PREDICTIONS, for articles with 3 to 5 independent partners: support by at least 1 partner 0.20 to 0.32 (per pair it is 0.111; with several partners it grows but less than independent draws would give, 1-(1-0.111)^4 = 0.38, because the same triples recur); by at least 2 partners 0.05 to 0.12; by at least 3 partners 0.01 to 0.05; control support by at least 1 partner under 0.02. For articles with 1 independent partner the at-least-1 rate is 0.09 to 0.13. A miss with at-least-2 under 0.03 would mean that triples backed by several publishers are too rare to seed Areas this way. Judge: match rates, not correctness.
T76 step 1

Score for T76 (projects/world-state/t76_support.py, runs/pulse/t76/t76_support.json; smoke test on 20 core articles passed first; full run 90 s on 8 processes; 3,460 core articles with at least 2 same-event partners, 3,982 articles parsed, 3,842 with triples, 29,151 triples; text keys, predicate lemma; unjudged). Share of an article's triples backed by at least 1, 2, 3 independent partners (different domain, shingle Jaccard under 0.30), by number of independent partners: 1 partner: 0.130, 0, 0; 2 partners: 0.179, 0.046, 0; 3 to 5 partners: 0.227, 0.095, 0.042; 6 or more partners: 0.352, 0.229, 0.163. Control with the same number of random articles: 0.001, 0.002, 0.004, 0.015 for at least 1, and at least 2 under 0.003 in every bucket. Triples backed by at least 2 independent partners: 2,843 of 29,151 (9.8 percent), by at least 3 about 1,500 (5.2 percent); 1,565 of the 2,843 are in the 6-or-more bucket. PREDICTIONS (L1525): 3 to 5 partners, at least 1: 0.20 to 0.32 HELD (0.227); at least 2: 0.05 to 0.12 HELD (0.095); at least 3: 0.01 to 0.05 HELD (0.042); control at least 1 under 0.02 HELD (0.004); 1 partner, at least 1: 0.09 to 0.13 MISSED by 0.0004 (0.1304), a rounding-sized miss. The failure case I named (at least 2 under 0.03) did not occur. READING: support grows with the number of independent publishers and is real (control near zero). About one triple in ten has two independent supporters and one in twenty has three, so a support-count rule for Areas is not too thin to use. But the support is concentrated: 55 percent of the triples with two supporters come from articles with six or more independent partners, i.e. the big stories many outlets cover. Areas seeded this way would be dominated by the day's large events, not by steady domains; a window of several days and a per-publisher cap (so one big event does not count 40 times) are needed. Whether 1 in 10 or 1 in 20 is enough for an Area is the owner's bar (T48). Judge: match rates, not correctness. Caveat: same 9,811 embedding-found pairs; small parser and text keys; both samples earlier gave 0.11 per pair.
T76 step 2
T76 step 3

T76 closed: support grows with the number of independent publishers (3 to 5 partners: 22.7 percent backed by one, 9.5 percent by two, 4.2 percent by three; 6 or more: 35, 23, 16); control under 1.5 percent; support is concentrated in big events. Four of five predictions held, one missed by 0.0004.

title: Map supported triples onto IPTC Media Topics
text: Map supported triples onto IPTC Media Topics
why: Seed Areas from a public ontology, no hand naming: see which ontology terms collect triples backed by 2+ independent publishers.
acceptance: Coverage and top-level consistency with the live topic reader for triples with 2+ independent supporters mapped to IPTC terms, with a random control and a first-draft Area table.
steps: Smoke test then full run, CPU

text: T77 started

Prediction for T77 (blind, CPU; input: the 2,843 triple rows with at least 2 independent supporters from T76, re-saved by a rerun of T76 that must reproduce T76's counts exactly; ontology: IPTC Media Topics, CC BY 4.0 per the licenceLink in the file, 1,394 terms, saved at /workspace/data/ontologies/iptc_mediatopic/ with sha256 prefix 16216d085254db34; mapping: bge-small-en-v1.5 cosine between the triple's evidence sentence and each term's label plus definition, best term wins; consistency: the mapped term's top-level category is among the categories of the live reader's top-two topics for the same article through topic_to_iptc_v1; control: a random term; threshold grid 0.40 to 0.60, primary 0.50). PREDICTIONS at the primary threshold 0.50: coverage 0.45 to 0.80 of triples; consistency with the article topic 0.50 to 0.75 against a random-term control of 0.08 to 0.25; at least 20 and at most 80 ontology terms with 5 or more mapped triples; at least 10 of the 17 top-level categories covered. A miss with consistency under 0.35 would mean sentence-to-definition mapping with this embedder is too noisy to seed Areas, and the next try is label-plus-path text or a different embedder. Judge: consistency with the live reader (which has its own error, about 0.80 on human labels), not truth. The reader abstains on some articles; those are excluded and the share is reported.
T77 step 1

Score for T77 (projects/world-state/t77_map.py, runs/pulse/t76b/t77_map.json and t77_area_draft.json; the chain first reran T76 with saving and its bucket counts equalled T76's exactly, so the input is the same 2,843 triple rows from 918 articles, 1,647 unique keys; IPTC Media Topics, 1,394 terms; bge-small-en-v1.5 on the evidence sentence against label plus definition; 90 s of compute; judge: consistency with the live reader's topic for the same article, which abstained on none). At the primary threshold 0.50: coverage 0.936; consistency 0.5024 against a random-term control 0.1871; 129 ontology terms with 5 or more mapped triples (73 with 10 or more); all 17 top-level categories covered. Over thresholds 0.40 to 0.60 the consistency runs 0.492, 0.492, 0.502, 0.535, 0.632 while sentence coverage runs 1.00, 1.00, 0.94, 0.67, 0.27 (keys-only coverage is higher, 0.79 at 0.60). PREDICTIONS (L1532): coverage 0.45 to 0.80 MISSED (0.936, the cosine threshold is not selective: nearly everything gets a term); consistency 0.50 to 0.75 HELD barely (0.5024); random control 0.08 to 0.25 HELD (0.187); 20 to 80 terms with 5 or more triples MISSED (129, too many fine terms); at least 10 of 17 top-level categories HELD (17); the failure case (consistency under 0.35) did not occur. READING: the mapping carries signal, about 2.7 times the random control at the primary threshold and 3.9 times at 0.60, but it is noisy: only about half the mapped triples land in a category consistent with their article's topic, and the reader itself agrees with human labels about 0.80, which caps what this check can show. Reading the draft table (first 14 terms): some are sensible (road incident, defendant, witness, arrest, impeachment, sentencing (criminal)), some are wrong at fine depth (bulldogging for a cousin testing positive, rifle shooting for a man selling ammunition, missing in action for ammunition manufacturing). As predicted at T76, the top terms are the big events of the window (McCabe, Roseanne Barr, a plow driver), not steady domains. The fine depth of the ontology (up to 5 levels, 1,394 terms) is the likely source of the noise; the next test restricts the ontology to its top levels. Judge: consistency with the live reader, not truth.
T77 step 2
T77 step 3

T77 closed: mapping triples with 2+ independent supporters onto IPTC terms gives 2.7 times chance consistency with the article topic (0.50 against 0.19) but is noisy at fine depth; 129 draft terms, mixed quality. Three of five predictions held.

title: Map to the top levels of the ontology only
text: Map to the top levels of the ontology only
why: T77 mapped to all 5 levels and was noisy at fine depth; test whether top levels give cleaner Areas.
acceptance: Consistency with the live topic reader and coverage for the same triples mapped to ontology depth 0, up to 1, and up to 2, next to T77's all-depth result.
steps: Smoke test then three runs, CPU

text: T78 started

Prediction for T78 (CPU; the same 2,843 supported triples and the same mapping method as T77, the ontology restricted to depth 0 only (17 top categories), depth up to 1 (148 terms) and depth up to 2 (about 715 terms); threshold 0.50 as the primary; consistency as defined in T77; T77 all-depth: coverage 0.936, consistency 0.502, control 0.187). PREDICTIONS at threshold 0.50: depth 0 only: consistency 0.55 to 0.75, coverage 0.45 to 0.90 (broad definitions have lower cosine with a sentence); depth up to 1: consistency 0.53 to 0.70; depth up to 2: consistency 0.50 to 0.62; consistency does not fall as depth is restricted (depth 0 at least as high as all-depth minus 0.02); terms with 5 or more mapped triples: depth 0 up to 17, depth up to 1: 25 to 80. A miss with depth-0 consistency under 0.45 would mean the noise is in the sentence-to-category similarity itself and not in the fine terms, which would call for a different embedder or zero-shot classifier. Judge: consistency with the live reader (about 0.80 against human labels), not truth.
T78 step 1

Score for T78 (projects/world-state/t77_map.py with DEPTH_MAX, runs/pulse/t76b/t77_map_d0.json, _d1, _d2; smoke test passed; 1m45s for all three; same 2,843 supported triples; judge: consistency with the live reader's topic, which abstained on none). At threshold 0.50, coverage / consistency / random control / terms with 5 or more triples: depth 0 only (17 terms) 0.172 / 0.378 / 0.110 / 11; depth up to 1 (148 terms) 0.657 / 0.315 / 0.103 / 56; depth up to 2 (715 terms) 0.883 / 0.447 / 0.160 / 106; all depths (1,394 terms, T77) 0.936 / 0.502 / 0.187 / 129. At every threshold the shallower ontologies are worse (depth up to 1 stays near 0.30 to 0.41). PREDICTIONS (L1538): depth 0 consistency 0.55 to 0.75 MISSED (0.378); depth 0 coverage 0.45 to 0.90 MISSED (0.172); depth up to 1 consistency 0.53 to 0.70 MISSED (0.315); depth up to 2 0.50 to 0.62 MISSED (0.447); consistency does not fall as depth is restricted MISSED (it falls); depth up to 1 has 25 to 80 terms with 5 or more triples HELD (56); depth 0 up to 17 HELD (11). So 2 of 7 held and the direction of my main prediction was wrong. READING: I expected coarse terms to be easier to match. The opposite holds: a sentence matches a specific term's definition better than a broad category's, so the nearest fine term, rolled up to its top-level category, is a better category assignment than matching the category directly (0.502 against 0.378). Fine terms work as anchors; the roll-up is where coarseness should come from. This also fits the owner's layers (Domain over Area over Capability): the fine terms are Capability candidates, their parents are Areas, the top level is the Domain. By my own pre-stated clause (depth-0 under 0.45) the noise is in the sentence-to-definition similarity itself; the live reader already supplies a Domain for each article at about 0.80 against human labels, so a better design may be to take the Domain from the reader and use the ontology only inside that Domain. That is the next test (T79). Judge: consistency with the live reader, not truth.
T78 step 2
T78 step 3

T78 closed: restricting the ontology to its top levels lowers consistency with the topic reader (depth 0: 0.378, up to 1: 0.315, up to 2: 0.447, all: 0.502); the opposite of my prediction. Fine terms anchor better; roll up for coarseness. Two of seven predictions held.

title: Domain from the reader, term from the ontology
text: Domain from the reader, term from the ontology
why: T78 showed the fine-term-then-roll-up mapping beats matching categories directly; test taking the Domain from the live reader and choosing the term only inside it.
acceptance: For the same fact (same triple key) stated in different articles: how often both instances map to the same term, the same second-level ancestor and the same top-level category, constrained to the reader's Domain versus unconstrained, with a random-pair baseline.
steps: Smoke test then full run, CPU

text: a criterion is over 200 characters
T79 started

Prediction for T79 (blind, CPU; the same 2,843 supported triple rows, ontology and sentence embeddings as T77; two assignments per row: unconstrained (best term over all 1,394) and constrained (best term among the descendants of the top-level categories of the live reader's top-two topics for that row's article); measure: for pairs of rows with the same triple key from different articles (at most 10 pairs per key, seed 7), the share mapped to the same term, to the same ancestor at depth 1, and to the same top-level category; baseline: the same number of random row pairs with different keys). PREDICTIONS: unconstrained same-term 0.25 to 0.50, same depth-1 ancestor 0.40 to 0.65, same top-level 0.55 to 0.80; constrained same-term 0.30 to 0.60 and at least 0.03 above unconstrained, same depth-1 ancestor 0.45 to 0.70, same top-level 0.65 to 0.90; random-pair baseline: same-term under 0.03, same top-level 0.08 to 0.25. A miss with constrained same-term not above unconstrained would mean the reader's Domain does not help reproducibility and the design stays ontology-only. Judge: agreement between assignments of the same fact, not truth; nothing here says the term is right.
T79 step 1

Score for T79 (projects/world-state/t79_constrain.py, runs/pulse/t76b/t79_constrain.json and t79_area_draft.json; smoke test passed; 49 s; the same 2,843 supported triple rows, 1,647 unique keys, 516 keys stated in 2 or more articles, 1,985 same-key pairs from different articles; the reader gave a Domain for every article; judge: agreement between the assignments of the same fact, not truth). Same-key pairs mapped to the same term / same depth-1 ancestor / same top-level category: unconstrained 0.666 / 0.707 / 0.758; constrained to the reader's Domain 0.677 / 0.771 / 0.868. Random pairs (different keys): unconstrained 0.010 / 0.046 / 0.107; constrained 0.012 / 0.059 / 0.137. Constrained draft: 121 terms with 5 or more triples (67 with 10 or more). PREDICTIONS (L1550): unconstrained same-term 0.25 to 0.50 MISSED (0.666, higher); unconstrained depth-1 0.40 to 0.65 MISSED (0.707); unconstrained top-level 0.55 to 0.80 HELD (0.758); constrained same-term 0.30 to 0.60 MISSED (0.677); constrained at least 0.03 above unconstrained on same-term MISSED (+0.011); constrained depth-1 0.45 to 0.70 MISSED (0.771); constrained top-level 0.65 to 0.90 HELD (0.868); random same-term under 0.03 HELD (0.010); random top-level 0.08 to 0.25 HELD (0.107). Four of nine held; I again set the ranges too low. READING: the assignment is reproducible across publishers: the same fact lands on the same ontology term 67 percent of the time and on the same top-level category 87 percent (constrained), against 1 and 14 percent for random pairs. Taking the Domain from the reader adds little at term level (+1 point) and more at the higher levels (+6 at depth 1, +11 at top level), as expected since it forces the category. LIMIT, stated plainly: reproducible is not correct. Sentences about the same fact are close in meaning, so a stable mapping is partly built in, and wrong terms are reproducibly wrong: the draft table still holds bulldogging (a sport term) for a cousin testing positive and missing in action for a gunman killing people. Nothing in T77 to T79 shows that a term is the right Area. No human gold exists for Areas; the one outside anchor that fits is MN-DS, whose human labels include IPTC level 2 (the same names as our depth-1 terms) for articles: a mapping of articles to depth-1 terms can be scored against it. That is the next test (T80). Judge: agreement between assignments of the same fact.
T79 step 2
T79 step 3

T79 closed: the same fact maps to the same ontology term 67 percent of the time across publishers (87 percent to the same top-level category when constrained to the reader's Domain), against 1 and 14 percent for random pairs; reproducible, not shown correct. Four of nine predictions held.

title: Ontology mapping against human IPTC level 2
text: Ontology mapping against human IPTC level 2
why: T77 to T79 showed the mapping is reproducible but not correct-by-evidence; MN-DS human labels include IPTC level 2, an outside check at the Area level.
acceptance: On MN-DS gold articles whose human level-2 label is an ontology depth-1 term: accuracy of the mapped depth-1 and top-level category against the human labels, with majority and random baselines.
steps: Smoke test then full run, CPU

text: T80 started

Prediction for T80 (blind, CPU; MN-DS fresh and fresh2 gold articles, deduplicated by id (the playbook warns that MN-DS ids collide; the earlier scorers used the same id keys), the article text the engine sees; IPTC Media Topics 1,394 terms; bge-small-en-v1.5 article text against label plus definition; best term rolled up to its depth-1 ancestor and top-level category; two variants: unconstrained, and constrained to the descendants of the live reader's top-two Domains; compared with the human level-1 and level-2 labels; scored on the items whose human level 2 is an ontology depth-1 term (82.8 percent of 2,897) and also over all items counting out-of-vocabulary ones as misses; baselines: always the most common level-2 label, and a random depth-1 term). PREDICTIONS on the in-vocabulary items: top-level (level 1) accuracy unconstrained 0.40 to 0.65, constrained 0.62 to 0.82 (the reader alone scores 0.68 top-one and 0.80 top-two lenient); level-2 accuracy unconstrained 0.12 to 0.30, constrained 0.15 to 0.35; majority-label baseline under 0.04; random depth-1 term under 0.02. A miss with constrained level-2 accuracy under 0.10 would mean the depth-1 ontology mapping is not a usable Area assignment even with the Domain given. Judge: MN-DS human labels (outside truth), lenient only where stated.
T80 step 1

Score for T80 (projects/world-state/t80_anchor.py, runs/pulse/t76b/t80_anchor.json; smoke test on 60 articles passed first; 103 s; MN-DS fresh and fresh2 gold articles deduplicated by id, 2,897 articles, the human level-2 label is an ontology depth-1 term for 2,399 of them (82.8 percent); outside truth, exact labels). In-vocabulary articles: unconstrained mapping level-1 accuracy 0.468, level-2 accuracy 0.266 (95 percent range 0.248 to 0.284); constrained to the live reader's Domain level-1 0.554, level-2 0.268 (0.252 to 0.285). All 2,897 articles (out-of-vocabulary counted as misses): level-2 0.220 unconstrained, 0.222 constrained. Baselines: always the most common level 2 ('market and exchange') 0.022; a random depth-1 term 0.008. PREDICTIONS (L1558): level-1 unconstrained 0.40 to 0.65 HELD (0.468); level-1 constrained 0.62 to 0.82 MISSED (0.554); level-2 unconstrained 0.12 to 0.30 HELD (0.266); level-2 constrained 0.15 to 0.35 HELD (0.268); majority baseline under 0.04 HELD (0.022); random under 0.02 HELD (0.008); the failure case (constrained level-2 under 0.10) did not occur. Five of six held. On the miss: I calibrated the level-1 range on the lenient scores of the reader (0.68 top-one, 0.80 top-two) but this metric is strict, the mapped top-level label must equal the single human label; the reader's strict top-one on this anchor is 0.454, so 0.554 is above it. That is my unit mix-up, not a surprise in the data. READING: against people, the embedding mapping assigns the right IPTC level-2 category to about 27 percent of articles (22 percent over everything), about 12 times the majority-label baseline and 34 times a random term, across 103 level-2 classes. Giving the mapping the reader's Domain lifts the top level by 9 points and level 2 by 0.3 points: the Domain helps the category, the fine choice inside it is the limit. It is a signal, not yet a usable Area assignment. This is the first outside-truth number for the Area layer. Judge: MN-DS human labels, exact. Caveats: the MN-DS ids collide in some rows per the playbook, the dedup is by id as in the earlier scorers; the ontology release (2026-09-30) is newer than the labels, which explains the 17 percent out-of-vocabulary level-2 names.
T80 step 2
T80 step 3

T80 closed: against MN-DS human IPTC level 2 the ontology mapping is right on 26.8 percent of in-vocabulary articles (majority baseline 2.2, random 0.8); the reader's Domain lifts the top level to 0.554 but not level 2. Five of six predictions held; the miss was my strict-versus-lenient mix-up.

title: Ontology mapping matrix: embedder and term text
text: Ontology mapping matrix: embedder and term text
why: T80 gave 27% exact level-2 against humans with one small embedder and label+definition text; find whether a larger embedder or richer term text lifts it, without overfitting the anchor.
acceptance: Level-2 accuracy against MN-DS human labels for 5 embedders and 2 term texts (10 arms); the arm chosen on the fresh file scored on the fresh2 file.

text: T81 started

Prediction for T81 (blind, CPU; the T80 setup unchanged except the arm: embedders bge-small-en-v1.5 (T80), bge-base-en-v1.5, bge-large-en-v1.5, e5-base-v2, gte-modernbert-base (this one may fail to load offline; a failed arm is reported, not hidden); term text 'def' (label + definition, as T80) or 'tree' (label + definition + the labels of its descendants up to two levels); scoring on the depth-1 ancestor of the best term against the human level 2, constrained to the reader's Domain, on in-vocabulary articles; SELECTION: the best arm on the fresh file (1,545 articles) is chosen, and only its score on the fresh2 file (1,352 articles, never used for choosing) is reported as the result; the other cells are reported as exploratory). Baseline arm on fresh2 is the T80 method. PREDICTIONS: the tree text beats the def text for bge-small by 0.02 to 0.08; bge-base beats bge-small by 0.01 to 0.05 on def; bge-large beats bge-base by 0.00 to 0.04; e5-base within plus or minus 0.03 of bge-base; the selected arm scored on fresh2 is 0.30 to 0.40 level-2 accuracy (T80 method on fresh2 about 0.26 to 0.28); no arm exceeds 0.45; top-3 accuracy of the selected arm 0.50 to 0.65. A miss with the selected arm under 0.28 on fresh2 would mean neither the embedder nor the term text is the limit, and the limit is the ontology granularity (131 depth-1 classes against 103 human classes). Judge: MN-DS human labels, exact.
T81 step 1

Process note 03:08: the first T81 chain ran under a 55 minute cap (timeout 3300 from 02:08) and the cap killed the runner at 03:03, in the middle of arm 10 (gte-modernbert with the tree text). Nine arms had finished with result files and no arm had errored; the runner was killed before it could close its heartbeat row, so the row said running for five minutes after the process was gone (the health line showed it as running until the overdue grace). My estimate of 25 to 40 minutes was too low: the chain needs about 60 minutes (bge-large and gte-modernbert are slow). I did not look at any score before the selection rule is applied. Arm 10 is rerun alone under a 40 minute cap with an exit trap that closes the row whatever happens. Lesson for chapter 16: size a chain's cap from the measured time per arm times the number of arms times 1.5, and close the row from an exit trap, not only at the end of the script.

Score for T81 (projects/world-state/t81_arm.py, runs/pulse/t81/t81_*.json and t81_summary.json; 10 arms, arm 10 rerun alone after the first chain's cap killed it; CPU; in-vocabulary MN-DS articles: 1,286 in fresh, 1,113 in fresh2; level-2 accuracy of the depth-1 ancestor of the best term, constrained to the reader's Domain; judge: MN-DS human labels, exact). SELECTION as pre-registered (best constrained top-1 on fresh): bge-large-en-v1.5 with label+definition, 0.285 on fresh. RESULT on the held-out fresh2: top-1 0.2534, top-3 0.4546, top-5 0.5508; the T80 method (bge-small, label+definition) on fresh2: 0.2525, 0.4456, 0.5409. So the chosen arm is 0.001 above the baseline method. All ten arms on fresh span 0.246 to 0.285 (top-1) and on fresh2 0.215 to 0.253; no arm is more than 0.03 from another. Exploratory table (fresh / fresh2, constrained top-1): bge-large def 0.285/0.253, bge-small def 0.282/0.253, bge-large tree 0.278/0.238, bge-base tree 0.275/0.248, bge-base def 0.275/0.237, bge-small tree 0.272/0.253, gte-modernbert tree 0.267/0.219, gte-modernbert def 0.263/0.235, e5-base def 0.255/0.217, e5-base tree 0.246/0.215. PREDICTIONS (L1566): tree beats def for bge-small by 0.02 to 0.08 MISSED (-0.010 on fresh, 0.000 on fresh2); bge-base beats bge-small on def by 0.01 to 0.05 MISSED (-0.007, -0.016); bge-large beats bge-base on def by 0.00 to 0.04 HELD (+0.010, +0.016); e5-base within plus or minus 0.03 of bge-base HELD (-0.020, -0.020); selected arm on fresh2 level-2 0.30 to 0.40 MISSED (0.253); no arm above 0.45 HELD; top-3 of the selected arm 0.50 to 0.65 MISSED (0.455). Three of seven held. The failure case I wrote down happened: the selected arm is under 0.28 on fresh2. READING by my own pre-stated clause: neither the embedder nor the term text is the limit of the 27 percent. Four embedder sizes and two term texts all land within 3 points of each other. Top-5 reaches 0.55: the human label is among the five nearest depth-1 terms in about half of the cases, so the nearest neighbours are the right neighbourhood but the ranking inside it does not separate them; the likely causes are the different granularity of the label sets (131 ontology depth-1 terms against 103 human classes, with 17 percent of human level-2 names not in this release of the ontology) and that plain similarity between a news text and a definition does not decide between neighbouring categories. The next lever is therefore not another embedder. Candidates: (a) rerank the five nearest terms with a model that reads both (local Clef, which needs the owner's yes because it runs on the GPU and would be used as a labeller), (b) a small classifier trained on pseudo-labels from an LLM teacher (the project's method), (c) accept about 27 percent at level 2 and use level 2 only as a soft label under the Domain. Judge: MN-DS human labels, exact. Caveat: choosing among ten arms on one file and reporting on the other keeps the reported number honest; the other nine cells are exploratory.
T81 step 2
T81 step 3

T81 closed: embedder size and term text do not move the ontology mapping (selected arm 0.253 on the held-out file against 0.2525 for the baseline method; all ten arms within 3 points); the limit is elsewhere. Three of seven predictions held.

title: CPU zero-shot rerank of the five nearest terms
text: CPU zero-shot rerank of the five nearest terms
why: T81: the right ontology term is in the top 5 about 55% of the time but top 1 only 25%; test whether a local zero-shot classifier on CPU separates the neighbours.
acceptance: Level-2 accuracy against MN-DS human labels for embedding top-1, zero-shot rerank of the top 5, and a fusion of both, on both files, with the top-5 ceiling.
steps: Smoke test then full run, CPU

text: T82 started

Prediction for T82 (blind, CPU only, no GPU, no labeller; the T81 setup with bge-small-en-v1.5 and label+definition term text, constrained to the live reader's Domain, candidates = the five nearest depth-1 ancestors per article; reranker = MoritzLaurer/deberta-v3-base-zeroshot-v2.0 (cached locally), hypothesis 'This text is about <label>.', entailment probability per candidate, article text truncated to 192 tokens; three scores: embedding top-1 (re-measured), zero-shot rerank, and a fixed-weight fusion (equal weight on the within-article z-scores of the cosine and of the entailment logit; the weights are fixed here, before any result); in-vocabulary MN-DS articles, both files, exact level-2 match; no selection among methods, all three reported). Ceiling: top-5 recall about 0.54 to 0.56, so no method can exceed that. PREDICTIONS: embedding top-1 on fresh2 0.24 to 0.27 (T81: 0.2525); zero-shot rerank top-1 on fresh2 0.20 to 0.34; fusion top-1 on fresh2 0.26 to 0.36, and at least 0.02 above the embedding top-1 on both files with probability about 0.6. A miss with fusion not above the embedding by 0.01 on fresh2 would mean a CPU zero-shot reranker does not separate the neighbouring categories either, and the remaining lever is an LLM teacher (needs the owner's yes). Judge: MN-DS human labels, exact. Runtime unknown: the smoke test measures it and the full run has a 50 minute cap with an exit trap.
T82 step 1

Scope change, 04:12, written before any result: the smoke test measured the reranker at 0.36 s per pair (255 pairs in 92 s at 12 threads), so the planned run over both MN-DS files (11,995 pairs) would take about 70 minutes, over my own 50 minute cap and over the 60 minute rule, and the script writes its result only at the end. I stopped my own first launch (4 processes, started 04:00, by verified pid; its exit trap closed the row as failed) and relaunched on fresh2 only (5,565 pairs, about 30 minutes). Consequences for the prediction at L1575: the claim 'at least 0.02 above the embedding on both files' cannot be scored and is dropped; the fresh2 claims stand unchanged (embedding 0.24 to 0.27, zero-shot 0.20 to 0.34, fusion 0.26 to 0.36); the fixed fusion weights are unchanged. A second smoke run on the changed script passed (32 articles, not evidence). Found while testing: my env variable TERM collides with the shell's terminal-type variable, so an unset TERM printed 'tmux-256color' as the term text in the output; the behaviour was the label+definition text, and the runner now sets TERM=def explicitly. Lessons: size the scope from the smoke timing before launching the full run, and never name a setting TERM.

Correction to the note above: the relaunch did not start at first. The new runner script was written without the executable bit and bash returned exit 126, so nothing ran for about two minutes while the note said it had relaunched (and the clock times in that note, 04:12 and 04:00, were also off: the first launch was at 03:57 and the relaunch attempt at 04:06). I fixed the permission and started the run at the time shown by the process list; the row was already registered as running, so the health line was wrong for those minutes. Lesson: after a launch, read the process list before writing that it runs.

Health check fix, 04:36: the run is healthy (pair 4,000 of 5,565 at 1,316 s, 0.33 s per pair) but the health line read 'nothing running' because the row is rewritten only at stage changes and goes overdue after 10 minutes. Added alive_pid to the rows: kit/live/health.py now counts a row as reporting while the process named by alive_pid exists (not pid, which the old poller code uses to close rows). Set alive_pid on this row. Documented in playbook chapter 16 section 8. The same gap would have hidden every long single-stage run; the T81 chain only avoided it because it rewrote the row per arm.

Score for T82 (projects/world-state/t82_rerank.py, runs/pulse/t82/t82_rerank.json; fresh2 only after the scope change recorded above; 5,565 pairs in 1,826 s; MN-DS in-vocabulary articles n 1,113; candidates = the five nearest depth-1 ancestors from bge-small with label+definition, constrained to the live reader's Domain; reranker deberta-v3-base-zeroshot-v2.0 entailment log-odds for 'This text is about <label>.'; fusion = equal-weight within-article z-scores of cosine and entailment log-odds, weights fixed before any result; judge: MN-DS human labels, exact level 2). Level-2 top-1: embedding alone 0.2525 (reproduces the T81 baseline arm exactly), zero-shot alone 0.2579, fusion 0.2956; top-5 ceiling 0.5409. PREDICTIONS (L1575): embedding top-1 0.24 to 0.27 HELD (0.2525); zero-shot rerank 0.20 to 0.34 HELD (0.258); fusion 0.26 to 0.36 HELD (0.296); fusion at least 0.02 above the embedding on fresh2 HELD (+0.043); the both-files claim was dropped at the scope change; the failure case (fusion not above the embedding by 0.01) did not occur. READING: the zero-shot model alone is no better than the embedding (+0.005), but the two together are: +4.3 points, because they err differently. That is the first lever in T77 to T82 that moves the level-2 match (the embedder, the term text and the ontology depth did not). It recovers about 4 of the 29 points between the embedding's 25 percent and the top-5 ceiling of 54 percent, so most of the gap remains. title: Condition: does more labelled data lift presence F1
text: Condition: does more labelled data lift presence F1
why: Owner asked (2026-11-10) whether the planned 1,500 Sonnet labels (about 650k tokens) are value driven. Cheapest check first: a learning curve on the existing labels, CPU only.
acceptance: Sealed presence F1 at 12.5, 25, 50 and 100 percent of the training labels, three subsample seeds each, with the seed spread; decide the labelling plan from the slope.
steps: Run the learning curve on CPU

text: T87 started

Prediction for T87 (blind, CPU, sparse presence head as in head_factory.py, label = at least one condition, sealed set 1,499 read once per point): sealed F1 at 0.5 rises with data: 12.5% 0.52 to 0.60, 25% 0.56 to 0.63, 50% 0.59 to 0.65, 100% 0.61 to 0.67 (the registered head scored about 0.64 to 0.66). The gain from 50% to 100% is at most 0.02, about the seed noise of 0.019 (p 0.6), which would mean more labels of this kind do not help and the 1,500-label plan is not worth its tokens as a way to raise F1. If the gain is above 0.03 (p 0.2), more labels help and the cheap targeted option (about 300 uncertain items) is tried first.
T87 step 1

Design correction before any run (sealed set must be read once): the curve points are scored on a fixed 15 percent dev slice of the labelled pool (F1 at 0.5, 3 subsample seeds per fraction); the sealed set is read once, at 100 percent of the training items, seed 1. The prediction ranges in the note above now apply to dev F1 at each fraction, and the registered head's sealed 0.64 to 0.66 for the single sealed read. The flat-or-rising call (gain from 50 to 100 percent at most 0.02, p 0.6) is unchanged.
T87 step 2

Score for T87 (prediction and correction above): result runs/pulse/t87/t87_curve.json (CPU, 4.7 s, 30,679 training items of which 3,672 positive, dev 5,413, sealed 1,499 read once). Dev F1 at 0.5, mean of 3 subsample seeds: 12.5% (3,834 items) 0.479, 25% 0.542, 50% 0.604, 100% 0.639; spread 0.026, 0.016, 0.008, 0.002. Sealed F1 at full data 0.6316. Against the ranges: 12.5% (0.52-0.60) WRONG, below; 25% (0.56-0.63) WRONG, below; 50% (0.59-0.65) right; 100% (0.61-0.67) right; sealed (0.64-0.66) WRONG by 0.008. Flat call WRONG: the gain from 50 to 100 percent is +0.035, above the 0.03 line (the p 0.2 branch). Per doubling the gain shrinks: +0.063, +0.062, +0.035. Reading: the curve is still rising but flattening. At the last slope, adding 1,500 labels (+4.9 percent) is worth about +0.003 F1 (0.035 x log2(1.049)), under the seed noise of 0.019; doubling the data to about 61,000 would be worth roughly +0.02 or less. So the planned 1,500 Sonnet labels (about 650k tokens) are not worth it as a way to raise presence F1. Limits: the label is 'at least one condition' under the old definitions, not rule A; the dev slice and sealed set are agreement with Sonnet, not outside truth; the extrapolation assumes the last slope holds.
T87 step 3

T87 closed: more labels of the current kind barely help presence F1 (about +0.003 for 1,500 more, doubling about +0.02). Do not spend the 650k tokens to raise F1 by volume. Relabelling under rule A is a different question (a changed target, not more data) and needs its own small, targeted test first.

After D20 (Condition definition A confirmed): contract_confirmed set true for the change field in rust_decider/fields.json (one line, backup kept). Route table result: change stays 'not admissible'. Reason: mark() admits only fields judged by a validator or outside gold; change is judged by Claude agreement (direction_cls.json, 3,871 stories, head 0.830 against always-up 0.784). None of the five local anchors (carb, checkthat_subj, few_nerd, maven_fact, mn_ds) labels direction; MAVEN-FACT labels whether a marked event happened and T27 found it does not transfer to free-text presence. So confirming the definition does not by itself make Condition answer 3 live; it needs a judge. Owner options: (a) a validator-style judge, e.g. a stated-in-text check as for size; (b) accept Claude agreement as the judge for this field, which lowers the bar; (c) leave it not admissible until an outside direction set exists. The planned 1,500-label run would not change this; labels are not the blocker (T87).

CORRECTION to L1637 (owner challenge 2026-11-10: the judging process was already defined): the three-way question about how Condition gets judged should not have been asked. Playbook 14 rule 3 already answers it: agreement is not accuracy, every field needs an outside anchor, even a one-sided one, or a written reason there is none. Rule 4 names the anchors in use: presence = MAVEN-FACT one-sided (T29), refutes a yes and never confirms one; direction has none. So option (b), accept Claude agreement as the judge, is excluded by rule 3, and (a) and (c) add nothing the rule does not already say. Recorded status, as the rule requires: Condition (change/direction): no outside anchor exists among carb, checkthat_subj, few_nerd, maven_fact, mn_ds; written reason: none of them labels direction; MAVEN-FACT labels whether a marked event happened and does not transfer to free-text presence (T27, T33); route marker stays 'not admissible' by design, not by a missing decision. title: Fix politics and religion mismatch in the reader constraint
text: Fix politics and religion mismatch in the reader constraint
why: T92 draft had no politics or religion terms. Cause found: specs/topic_to_iptc_v1.json names the categories 'politics' and 'religion and belief' but the IPTC top-level labels are 'politics and government' and 'religion', so the reader constraint masks every term for items whose reader categories are only those.
acceptance: Alias fix in the shared mapping code; T80 and T92 rerun in new folders; old results labelled, not overwritten; effect on exact-match accuracy and on the Area draft measured
steps: Correction note, then alias fix and smoke
Rerun T80 mapping with the fix, score

text: T93 started

Correction (found 2026-11-10 while checking why the T92 draft has no politics): specs/topic_to_iptc_v1.json maps reader topics to category names that include 'politics' and 'religion and belief' (the MN-DS vocabulary), but the IPTC Media Topics top-level labels are 'politics and government' and 'religion'. The reader constraint in t77_map.py (art_cats, used by t79_constrain.py and the T92 run), t80_anchor.py and t81_arm.py (and t84_area_head.py and t82_rerank.py, which reuse t81 pieces) tests whether a term's top-level label is in the reader's category set. For an item whose reader categories are only politics or religion the test matches nothing, every term is masked, and the argmax falls to the first term in the ontology; for mixed items such as diplomacy the constraint silently drops the politics part. Evidence: the T92 draft has 0 terms under any politics top-level, while a 100-article smoke of T93 shows the reader tags 22 percent of supported-triple articles (13 percent of a random pool) as politics topics, so the articles are present and the loss is in the mapping. Affected and not yet re-measured: constrained arms in T79 (L1551 reading that the constraint helps only at the top level), T80 and T81 exact-match scores, the T82 and T83 fusion figure, the T84 pseudo-labels, and the T92 draft and its lean toward crime and sport. Unaffected: unconstrained arms, the topic anchor scoring against MN-DS labels (it compares reader topic to the MN-DS names directly). Nothing is overwritten: reruns go to new folders and the old files stay as recorded, labelled before the fix. Fix is an alias in one shared helper, applied in the three loading scripts.

engine.name: BitMob Expert 1
engine.how: Every item is read by fast linear models on word counts and static word vectors. About a third of items, the ones a cheap first pass flags, also go through a small encoder: MongoDB's mdbr-leaf-mt (22.6M parameters, 6 layers, 512 tokens). Long articles are cut into chunks. From 2026-11-04 the reader is v6b-student: the same sparse parts plus a fine-tuned copy of that encoder (22.6M parameters, distilled from 16,000 Sonnet labels) that reads story type, topic, condition presence and which condition in one pass; 15 ms typical on one CPU thread. From 2026-11-05 the same reader also serves per-condition heads for four kinds (air pollution, biodiversity loss, civil unrest, cyber insecurity) and a direction head for biodiversity loss, on the same embedding, 16.6 ms median over HTTP (service pulse_reader, route /v1/pulse; nothing calls it yet). Since 2026-11-08 an optional pair of sparse heads (topic and story type) can answer first and skip the encoder when both are confident; off by default (ledger L1137).
engine.why: Linear models alone already match Sonnet on story type. The encoder adds the most on which-condition and topic. Chosen from the full field of 215 scored models: in our size class it ties on every Pulse field, is about 40% faster than bge-small (95% of reads under 23 ms), uses 80 MB less memory, and joins related articles better. Adopted after one scoring on the sealed 1,499 items (ledger L771): better than v5-leaf on story type, topic and real conditions found; condition is still Not ready.
engine.teacher: claude-sonnet-5-5 (frozen guideline). Agreement with Sonnet, never accuracy: no human gold.
engine.bar_note: Owner's working figure: agreement of 80% or more on the items it answers.
engine.rule: Ready needs all four: (1) counted over every item, a skipped item is a miss, and the low end of the 95% range is 80% or more; (2) the low end beats always guessing the most common answer; (3) if the field finds something rare, it finds 80% or more of the real cases; (4) 30+ items, and a step that depends on an earlier one waits until that one is Ready. Partial = 80% or more only on the items it answers (it answers at least half). Not yet = anything else. Later phase = not built. Exception (owner, 2026-11-05): direction and size are read from the story text and scored on their own; they do not wait on condition.
